name: Santería
info: Santería, also called Regla de Ocha, Regla Lucumí or Lucumí, is an Afro-Cuban religion that arose in the late 19th century from Yoruba religion, Catholicism and Spiritism, and is known for its oricha, its initiations and its drumming ceremonies.

facts.origin: Cuba, in the cities of the west of the island, in the late 19th century, from the traditional Yoruba religion brought by enslaved West Africans, Roman Catholicism and Spiritism.
facts.founder: none: it has no single founder. It formed among Afro-Cuban communities, and a trained priesthood in the first houses of worship gave new initiates a degree of standardisation.
facts.scriptures: none: there is no key sacred text. Knowledge passes mostly by oral teaching and by taking part in rites; since at least the 20th century some initiates have kept notebooks (libretas), and the oricha are known through stories called patakís.
facts.followers: The number of initiates is estimated to be in the high hundreds of thousands. For the early 21st century two scholars estimated that about 8% of Cubans, between 800,000 and 900,000 people, were initiates. The American Religious Identification Survey of 2001 estimated about 22,000 practitioners in the United States.

t: Santería teaches a creator, Olodumare, and spirits called oricha who are equated with Roman Catholic saints; each person is believed to be born to one oricha, the owner of their head.
The religion formed among enslaved West Africans, most of them Yoruba, and their descendants in Cuba, where Roman Catholicism was the only religion the colonial government allowed.
It has no central authority and no key sacred text; each ilé, or house-temple, is largely autonomous, and membership requires initiation.
dyk: Santería's central public ritual is a drumming ceremony, the toque de santo, played on double-headed batá drums that are regarded as sacred; each ceremonial drum must be born from an existing one, so that drums form lineages.
ev: The first enslaved Africans arrive in Cuba
The first houses teaching Santería emerge in urban parts of western Cuba
Cuba becomes an independent republic whose constitution enshrines freedom of religion
Rómula Lachatañeré's Manuel de santería is published, the first scholarly attempt to understand Santería as a religion
The Cuban Revolution brings to power a government committed to state atheism, which takes a negative view of Santería
The Ooni of Ife Olubuse II visits Cuba, reinforcing links with Yoruba religion
Cuba's constitution is amended to declare the country secular rather than atheist
In Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah the United States Supreme Court rules that animal cruelty laws aimed at Santería are unconstitutional

sections.origins:
Santería developed among Afro-Cuban communities after the Atlantic slave trade of the 16th to 19th centuries. The first enslaved Africans reached Cuba in 1511, the largest numbers came in the 19th century, full emancipation came in 1886, and between 702,000 and 1 million enslaved Africans were brought to the island in all. Most came from West Africa between the modern states of Guinea and Angola, and the great plurality were Yoruba, from the area of modern Nigeria and Benin. In Cuba the enslaved were grouped into naciones, often by port of embarkation, and Yoruba speakers were counted in the Lucumí nation.

Roman Catholicism was the only religion legally permitted under Spanish rule, and instruction in it was typically perfunctory. Traditional deities perhaps continued to be venerated in cabildos de nación, associations of Africans and their descendants that the establishment regarded as a means of control, and it is probable that priests of different West African orisha interacted there and began to develop a new system. Fewer than twenty of the hundreds of orisha worshipped in West Africa became prominent in Santería, and separate cults were reconstituted as one system with a newly standardised pantheon.

In the final decades of the 19th century Spiritism, based on the ideas of the French writer Allan Kardec, gained ground in Cuba and influenced Santería. The earliest houses teaching it emerged in urban parts of western Cuba in the late 19th century. Mary Ann Clark described it as “a new religious system”, though it drew on older West African cults.
sections.beliefs:
Santería teaches the existence of an overarching divinity, Olodumare, also called Olofi or Olorun, who practitioners believe created the universe but takes little interest in human affairs. Beneath this divinity are the oricha, also called ocha or santos, who usually take their names and attributes from Yoruba deities and are equated with Roman Catholic saints: Changó with Santa Barbara, Babalú Ayé with Saint Lazarus, Ochún with Cuba's patron saint, Our Lady of Charity. Some oricha are believed to have been created before humanity and others to have been humans who became oricha. They are not regarded as wholly benevolent. Each is associated with an aspect of nature or life, among them Eleguá, guardian of crossroads, Ogun of iron and war, Yemaya of the sea and Orula of divination.

Practitioners hold that each person is born to a particular oricha, who “rules the head” and influences their personality. The oricha are approached with offerings, ceremonies and divination, and aché, a force believed to permeate the universe, can be raised through song, dance, drumming and sacrifice. Santería also venerates the spirits of the dead, the egun, who are offered water and consulted at all ceremonies. The religion is described as non-dualistic: all things are seen as complementary and relative rather than divided between good and evil.

It is described as practice-oriented, with ritual correctness regarded as more important than belief. Practitioners take part in the religion's rites as work, trabajo.
sections.texts:
Santería has no key sacred text and no strict orthodoxy. It is a largely oral tradition, and santeros and santeras often teach in a non-verbal manner, encouraging initiates to learn by taking part in ritual activity. Since at least the 20th century some initiates have written down material relevant to the practice in notebooks called libretas, which may be shared with their own initiates or kept private.

The stories of the oricha, including their origin myths, are called patakís. Divination draws on them: the dilogún, in which cowrie shells are cast, requires a knowledge of the patakie stories. Ifá, the most complex and prestigious system of divination used in the religion, has a separate existence from Santería but shares its mythology and conception of the universe. Its high priests are babalawos.

The ritual language is Lucumí, sometimes called la lengua de los orichas, regarded as a divine language through which practitioners can contact the deities. It derives from Yoruba, though it has become “increasingly fragmented and unintelligible” since the 19th century. Most initiates know tens or hundreds of Lucumí words and phrases, and in the early 21st century some practitioners have studied Yoruba to understand the original meaning of Lucumí words. Praise songs for the oricha are sung at ceremonies, each oricha being associated with particular songs and rhythms.
sections.spread:
From the late 19th century urban-to-rural migration spread Santería elsewhere in Cuba, and in the 1930s it probably arrived in Santiago de Cuba, at the eastern end of the island. In Cuba it has always been a primarily urban phenomenon, predominating in the provinces of La Habana and Matanzas, though it is also found in rural areas.

The Cuban Revolution of 1959 fuelled emigration to the United States, Puerto Rico, Mexico, Colombia and Venezuela. Santería was present in the United States by the 1940s and increased its presence afterwards, clustering in Florida, California, New Jersey and New York and attracting Latino, European American and African American practitioners. In Mexico it has a particular presence in Veracruz and Mexico City, in Canada it centres on Toronto, and in Europe houses have formed in Spain and Germany. It is a non-proselytising religion that nonetheless accepts new followers.

In the second half of the 20th century links grew with related traditions in West Africa and the Americas. The Ooni of Ife Olubuse II visited Cuba in 1987, a Yoruba Cultural Association was permitted in the early 1990s, and various practitioners travelled to Nigeria to study traditional Yoruba religion. A process of yorubización emerged, which sought to remove Roman Catholic elements, and critics of it valued Santería's syncretism. In 1970 the black nationalist activist Walter King moved his followers from Harlem to Sheldon, South Carolina, where they founded the Yoruba Village of Oyotunji.
sections.community:
The ilé is both the house-temple, usually the home of a santero or santera, and the community that meets there; each ilé is largely autonomous. Practitioners are called creyentes, believers, and a non-initiate is an aleyo. Most ilés are founded by a santero or santera who has attracted a following. Initiates are the godchildren (ahijados) of their padrino or madrina, a relationship central to the religion's social organisation, and members of a house regard one another as a familia de santo. Initiation, kariocha, takes seven days plus two days of preparation, is costly, and is often concealed from non-initiates. Women can hold the highest leadership positions, though restrictions apply to them while menstruating.

After the republic's founding in 1898, Santería was never legislated against, but throughout the first half of the 20th century campaigns were launched against it, encouraged by a press that promoted allegations that white children were being abducted and murdered in its rituals. Afro-Cuban practices were called brujería, witchcraft. Fernando Ortiz, in 1906, saw Santería as a barrier to the integration of Afro-Cubans and recommended its suppression.

After 1959 practitioners faced police harassment, were denied Communist Party membership and needed police permission for rituals. In the 1990s the government selectively supported Afro-Cuban traditions, partly to boost tourism, and in 1991 the Party admitted religious members; Santería began to be practised more openly. Many practitioners also identify as Roman Catholics, Spiritists or members of other religions.
sections.legacy:
Santería is sometimes described in Cuba as “the national religion”. It is the best known and most popular of the Afro-Cuban religions, which include Palo, Abakuá and Arará, and it shares its origins in Yoruba religion with Haitian Vodou and Brazilian Candomblé, sometimes called its sister religions. It remains most common among working-class Afro-Cuban communities, though people of other classes and backgrounds practise it, and it has absorbed elements from cultures it has met, among them Chinese migrants in Cuba and, in North America, Central American and Mexican religions and New Age practice.

Its animal sacrifice has caused concern among non-practitioners and has brought adherents into conflict with the law. In 1993 the United States Supreme Court, in Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah, ruled that animal cruelty laws targeted at Santería were unconstitutional. Christian views of the religion have been largely negative, and the Roman Catholic clerical establishment in Cuba has opposed it over the centuries. In Veracruz, Catholic organisations protested the Santería elements of the International Afro-Caribbean Festival launched in 1994, and they had been cut by 1998.

Santería has also been taken up in other media: Gloria Rolando's film Oggún appeared in 1992, Celia Cruz recorded “Que viva Chango”, and a Cuban band named itself Los Orichas. In the United States it influenced the revival of Louisiana Voodoo in the late 20th century.

summary: Santería is an Afro-Cuban religion that formed in western Cuba in the late 19th century from Yoruba religion, Catholicism and Spiritism. Its practitioners venerate the oricha, spirits equated with Catholic saints, in autonomous houses entered by initiation. Marginalised in Cuba for much of the 20th century, it spread abroad after 1959.
